passage:
Dear Farhan,
Thank you for sending the deck this morning. The customer story on slide three is the strongest part: the delayed-parcel example made the problem clear to me in ten seconds. One thing to change: on slide seven the sales chart has no label on the vertical axis, and someone in the room will ask what the numbers mean before you can make your point. Could you add the label and one line saying what the chart shows? Then people will not lose the thread. I am free tomorrow at ten if you would like me to look again. You are close. 🙂
Kishore

qa.q: Which slide has the chart with no label on the vertical axis?
qa.a: Slide seven has the sales chart with no label on the vertical axis.

qa.q: What does Kishore want for Farhan by offering to look again tomorrow?
qa.a: Kishore wants Farhan to feel supported and able to act, and the closing line "You are close" shows encouragement instead of criticism.

qa.q: What could Farhan do first after reading the letter?
qa.a: Farhan could add a label to the vertical axis on slide seven and a one-line takeaway, then send the deck back to Kishore for a second look.

qa.q: How might Farhan feel reading this compared with a comment like "Not good enough"?
qa.a: Farhan would probably feel respected and clear about the next step, since one strong part and one exact spot with a reason leave little to defend.

grounding: Shows a reviewer naming what works, pointing to a concrete spot and giving the reason in a kind, timely note.

subtype: Giving feedback that can be used [Response]
passage: Same day, always. If I wait a week, the person has already made up a story about my silence. So when a junior sends me a report, I read it once for what works and say that first, honestly. This time it was the clean summary table. Then I pick one spot, page four, the paragraph with three numbers and no source, and I say why: a reader will doubt the rest if they cannot trace it. I suggest adding a source line. Then I stop. Sangeeta, you asked if it feels awkward. A bit. But when they come back with the fix and a question, I know it landed. Shankar

qa.q: Which page has the paragraph with three numbers and no source?
qa.a: Page four has the paragraph with three numbers and no source.

qa.q: How does Shankar feel about giving feedback, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Shankar feels a little awkward but sure of the approach, saying it feels awkward yet judging by the juniors who come back with the fix and a question that it lands.

qa.q: What makes Shankar's feedback something a junior can act on?
qa.a: It names what works first, points to one concrete paragraph, gives the reason and suggests a fix, all on the same day.

qa.q: What might the junior who sent the report feel if Shankar waited a week to reply?
qa.a: They might make up a story about the silence and expect the worst, which is why Shankar replies the same day.

grounding: Shows a reviewer who gives specific, timely, kind feedback with a named strength, one concrete spot and a reason.

passage: I was in the design review when Bhavna gave feedback on Akash's website mock-up, and I've been thinking about it since. She didn't start with problems. "The colours feel calm, which suits a clinic. That works." Then she pointed at the screen. "This booking button is grey and at the bottom. Patients in a hurry won't find it. Make it the brightest thing on the page and move it up." And then, "Why it matters: most visits start from phones." That was it. Three minutes. Akash didn't argue once. He just nodded, took notes and asked if orange would work. In other reviews I've watched people defend every pixel. I can't say how Akash felt inside, but he didn't look defensive.

qa.q: What colour was the booking button in Akash's mock-up?
qa.a: The booking button was grey.

qa.q: What might Akash have felt during Bhavna's feedback?
qa.a: He seemed calm and open, not defensive, likely feeling respected because she started with what worked.

qa.q: Which parts of Bhavna's feedback made it usable?
qa.a: She named what worked, pointed to a concrete spot to change, and gave the reason: most visits start from phones.

qa.q: How does the person watching the review see Bhavna's approach?
qa.a: The watcher sees it as unusually effective, contrasting it with other reviews where people defend every pixel.

grounding: An observer describes a reviewer who names what works, points to one concrete change and explains why, so the receiver acts instead of defending.

passage:
Monday. Lokesh, twenty-six, led a small content team. Mahima, a new writer, sent her first article. Last year Lokesh would have written "needs work" and moved on. This time he wrote: "Your opening story is great; it pulls the reader in. Paragraph four has three statistics in a row, and it's hard to follow. Pick the strongest one; readers remember one number, not three."
Wednesday. Mahima sent the revision. Paragraph four had one number and a short example. She had also trimmed paragraph six on her own.
Friday. Mahima asked, "Can you review my next one the same way?" Lokesh smiled. Her second draft needed half the changes of the first.

qa.q: Which paragraph had three statistics in a row?
qa.a: Paragraph four had three statistics in a row.

qa.q: What does Mahima's request on Friday suggest about how she felt?
qa.a: It suggests she felt encouraged and respected by the specific feedback, and trusted it enough to want more.

qa.q: What did Lokesh do differently from last year, and why did it help?
qa.a: He named what worked, pointed to paragraph four and explained why, which gave Mahima something clear to act on.

qa.q: How might Lokesh feel when the second draft needs half the changes?
qa.a: Lokesh would likely feel pleased and proud, seeing that the specific feedback helped Mahima learn fast.

grounding: Shows over a week a team lead giving specific, timely, kind feedback that the new writer can act on.

subtype: Giving feedback that can be used [Response]
passage: Anand, you've just become a manager, so listen to your Dadu. When I was twenty-five, I ran the printing section at a newspaper in Guwahati. I'm Bhupen, and in those days I was known for shouting "Wrong!" at the young typesetters. They hated me, and nothing improved. One day my own boss showed me a better way. He picked up a page and said, "The headline is sharp. But this column is two lines too long, so the photo gets cut. Shorten it here, because readers look at photos first." I tried that with my typesetters. Something good, one exact place, and why. Within a month, the errors halved. And people stopped hiding when I walked in.

qa.q: Where did Bhupen run the printing section?
qa.a: At a newspaper in Guwahati.

qa.q: How did Bhupen feel when the typesetters stopped hiding?
qa.a: He likely felt relieved and proud, seeing that his new way of giving feedback earned respect as well as better work.

qa.q: Which choice in the story changed the results?
qa.a: Switching from shouting "Wrong!" to naming something good, one exact place and why, which halved the errors in a month.

qa.q: How did the young typesetters experience Bhupen's old way?
qa.a: The typesetters hated it and hid when he walked in, and nothing improved because they didn't know what to change.

grounding: An elder recalls learning to give feedback that names what works, points to a concrete spot and says why.

subtype: Giving feedback that can be used [Response]
passage: The exhaust fan in the café kitchen in Shillong had died that morning, and service started in fifteen minutes. In the heat and clatter, Ganga held out a spoon of her new pumpkin soup, the first dish she had created for the menu. Devika tasted it and didn't make her wait. "The ginger and smoked chilli on top, that's the best thing in it. Keep that exactly." She tasted again. "The salt builds, though. By the last spoonful it's too much, because the stock is already salted. Go easy on the salt at the end. And the bread cubes go soft in two minutes, so serve them on the side." Ganga's shoulders came down from where they had been hunched. "Less salt at the end, bread on the side. Got it." She adjusted the pot while Devika checked the tandoor. By the first order, the soup went out with a little bowl of crisp cubes beside it.

qa.q: Why did Devika say the salt built up by the last spoonful?
qa.a: Because the stock is already salted.

qa.q: How was Ganga feeling while holding out the spoon, and how did that change?
qa.a: Ganga was nervous, shoulders hunched over her first menu dish, and then relieved once the comments came clear and kind.

qa.q: What made Devika's comments easy to act on?
qa.a: She named what worked, the ginger and chilli, pointed to two exact changes, the salt at the end and the bread on the side, and said why, all straight away.

qa.q: What would change if Devika had only said "too salty, fix it" in the rush?
qa.a: Ganga might have felt stung and guessed at the fix, perhaps losing the topping that worked, with no time before service to find out.

grounding: Illustrates a reviewer giving quick, specific, kind feedback that names what works, points to exact changes and explains why, so it is acted on at once.
